figures.title: Income testing distributions · preferred gradient boosting in blue
figures.caption: Survey-weighted CPHS testing histograms. Positive income is shown in natural-log rupees. Black: observed; blue: preferred gradient boosting; orange: random forest; green: elastic net where shown. Each panel retains its original positive-value sample. This distribution figure comes from an earlier evaluation than the current metric table; its testing sample is separate.

figures.title: Positive wealth and debt: baseline aggregates
figures.caption: Survey-weighted AIDIS testing-sample histograms of positive amounts. The horizontal axis is the natural logarithm of rupees, with bins from 4 to 18 in steps of 0.25; the vertical axis is density within the plotted range. Zero annotations use all testing households with non-positive amounts; the predicted annotation refers to the blue quantile-mapped or piecewise series.

method_notes.ols: Ordinary least squares fits a linear relationship between transformed income and household predictors. Total income uses logs; other income targets use the inverse hyperbolic sine. The model uses survey weights and the common household testing split. It has no regularization parameter.
method_notes.lasso: Lasso fits a linear income model with an absolute-value penalty that can set coefficients to zero. The Stata comparison chooses its penalty using five-fold cross-validation; the aggregate metrics workbook does not record the selected penalty.
method_notes.hgb: Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially to reduce prediction error. Income uses at most 500 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping. Wealth uses a two-part model: a positive-amount classifier with at most 400 iterations and a log-amount regressor with at most 500, both at learning rate 0.06. Wealth ownership thresholds are calibrated using training data; positive amounts use Duan smearing.
method_notes.rf: Random forest averages predictions across independently grown trees. The income and two-part wealth specifications use 300 trees, at least five observations per leaf, and 30% of predictor columns at each split. Wealth uses separate classifiers and positive log-amount regressions, with calibrated participation thresholds and Duan smearing.
method_notes.enet: Elastic net fits a linear model with both absolute-value and squared-coefficient penalties. Income uses five-fold cross-validation over mixing values 0.1, 0.5, 0.9 and 1.0, with at most 5,000 solver iterations. The wealth ownership stage uses L1 logistic regression with C=1, the liblinear solver and at most 300 iterations; its positive log-amount stage uses the same five-fold mixing grid and at most 3,000 iterations, followed by Duan smearing.
method_notes.stata: The Stata wealth model first predicts whether an amount is positive, then fits OLS to the log amount among positive holders. The first part uses logit with up to 200 iterations, falling back to a linear probability model when logit fails or drops more than 1% of the estimation sample. Participation thresholds are calibrated on training data, and Duan smearing converts log amounts back to rupees.
method_notes.hgbq: Mapped gradient boosting retains the two-part gradient-boosting prediction and applies a monotone quantile map to positive predicted amounts. The map is fitted on training households and aligns predicted amounts with the weighted observed distribution while preserving ranks. This addresses the compression of wealth under conditional-mean prediction.
method_notes.hgbqp: Amount and participation mapping extends quantile-mapped gradient boosting by mapping the prediction score distribution across surveys. Amount mappings use training data; participation mappings use the AIDIS reference score distribution before applying calibrated thresholds.
method_notes.hgbqph: The preferred wealth route combines mapped amounts and participation with a separate gold hurdle model. Gold ownership excludes the gold-saving indicator that reveals ownership in AIDIS. The ownership classifier uses at most 400 boosting iterations and learning rate 0.06, with out-of-fold calibration; positive gold amounts are rank-mapped to observed training amounts. Non-gold components inherit the amount-and-participation mapped route.
method_notes.hpw: Piecewise housing prediction separates dwelling ownership from the amount among owners. It excludes the house-ownership indicator from predictors, maps CPHS participation scores to the AIDIS reference, and rank-maps positive amounts using the training distribution. The classifier uses at most 400 iterations and the log-amount regressor at most 500, both with learning rate 0.06; calibration uses three-fold out-of-fold predictions.
method_notes.apcbin: The consumption-bin benchmark splits the weighted training consumption distribution into 50 bins. Within each bin it estimates the ratio of mean consumption to mean income, then predicts income using household consumption and that ratio. No other household predictors enter.
method_notes.cbin: The consumption-bin wealth benchmark splits weighted training consumption into 50 bins. It predicts wealth using consumption multiplied by the within-bin ratio of mean wealth to mean consumption. This is a one-variable benchmark rather than a fitted tree model.
method_notes.rankmap: Consumption-rank mapping assigns each household the target value at the same weighted percentile as its consumption. The empirical mapping is fitted using training households. It preserves the target distribution but does not use demographic or financial predictors.
method_notes.hgb_rw: Reweighted gradient boosting uses a classifier of survey membership to reweight CPHS toward AIDIS before fitting the income model. The survey probability is clipped to [0.001, 0.999] and converted to odds. The income regressor keeps the gradient-boosting settings: at most 500 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping.
method_notes.hgb_noc: This gradient-boosting robustness specification excludes consumption from the predictor set. Other income-model settings remain at most 500 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping, using the same testing households.
method_notes.qgbd: Quantile gradient boosting fits the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th conditional percentiles, then draws a uniform percentile and interpolates between them. Each quantile fit uses at most 300 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and maximum depth three. Draws retain distributional variation rather than minimizing point-prediction error.
method_notes.wbin: The two-part wealth-bin benchmark sorts training households into 50 weighted consumption bins. Each bin supplies an ownership rate and the ratio of mean positive wealth to mean consumption among holders. Predictions combine the calibrated ownership threshold with consumption multiplied by that ratio; no Duan correction or demographic predictors are used.
method_notes.hgb_c2: This gradient-boosting specification replaces the standard consumption measure with alternative total consumption. The income alternative uses at most 250 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping; the two-part wealth alternative uses at most 200 iterations in each part, the same learning rate and early stopping.
method_notes.ols_c2: This OLS specification replaces the standard consumption predictor with alternative total consumption. It otherwise uses the same linear-model design and testing households as the OLS comparison; no regularization penalty is applied.
method_notes.hgb_nd1: This gradient-boosting specification replaces the standard consumption measure with nondurable consumption, definition 1. The income alternative uses at most 250 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping; the two-part wealth alternative uses at most 200 iterations in each part, the same learning rate and early stopping.
method_notes.ols_nd1: This OLS specification replaces the standard consumption predictor with nondurable consumption, definition 1. It otherwise uses the same linear-model design and testing households as the OLS comparison; no regularization penalty is applied.
method_notes.hgb_nd2: This gradient-boosting specification replaces the standard consumption measure with nondurable consumption, definition 2. The income alternative uses at most 250 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping; the two-part wealth alternative uses at most 200 iterations in each part, the same learning rate and early stopping.
method_notes.ols_nd2: This OLS specification replaces the standard consumption predictor with nondurable consumption, definition 2. It otherwise uses the same linear-model design and testing households as the OLS comparison; no regularization penalty is applied.
method_notes.hgb_uce: This gradient-boosting specification replaces the standard consumption measure with usual consumption expenditure. The income alternative uses at most 250 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping; the two-part wealth alternative uses at most 200 iterations in each part, the same learning rate and early stopping.
method_notes.ols_uce: This OLS specification replaces the standard consumption predictor with usual consumption expenditure. It otherwise uses the same linear-model design and testing households as the OLS comparison; no regularization penalty is applied.
method_notes.hgb_sp: This gradient-boosting specification replaces the standard consumption measure with self-production income. The income alternative uses at most 250 iterations, learning rate 0.06 and early stopping; the two-part wealth alternative uses at most 200 iterations in each part, the same learning rate and early stopping.
method_notes.ols_sp: This OLS specification replaces the standard consumption predictor with self-production income. It otherwise uses the same linear-model design and testing households as the OLS comparison; no regularization penalty is applied.
method_notes.ols_noc: This OLS robustness specification excludes consumption from the predictor set and keeps the same testing households as the income-model comparison.
method_notes.income_preferred: Gradient boosting is the preferred income model because it has the strongest fit among the standard multivariate comparison models on the shared CPHS testing sample.
method_notes.wealth_preferred: Mapped amounts with the piecewise gold model are preferred because they restore wealth dispersion and separate gold ownership from positive amounts, preserving the distribution and ownership margins used in household classification.
method_notes.predictors: Current prediction specifications describe age groups rather than the household head: counts below 18, at 18–24, at 25–64 and at 65+, men and median age among 25–64-year-olds, education, religion, caste, employment type, state and district. Financial predictors include consumption, livestock, tractors and cars, bank accounts, saving in shares and mutual funds, borrowing sources and purposes, and vehicle counts. Wealth models additionally include debt service. The headline excludes indicators identified as non-comparable across surveys, including house ownership, two-wheeler ownership, fixed deposits and gold saving. The older AIDIS characterization retains head-based demographics; a complete current predictor-by-HtM summary has not yet been exported.
method_notes.tp_lin: A two-part linear model separates whether self-production income is positive from its amount when positive.
method_notes.tp_lin_cal: The calibrated two-part linear specification separates participation and positive amounts for self-production income.
method_notes.tp_hgb: A two-part gradient-boosting specification separates participation and positive amounts for self-production income.
method_notes.tp_hgb_cal: The calibrated two-part gradient-boosting specification separates participation and positive amounts for self-production income.
method_notes.tp_hgb_draw: The two-part gradient-boosting draw specification represents the distribution of self-production income rather than only its conditional mean.

testing_notes.income: CPHS holds out 20% of households for testing; the current income metrics use 25,759 testing households. Models use the same split. Total-income errors are in logs; component-income errors use the inverse hyperbolic sine.
testing_notes.wealth: AIDIS holds out 20% of households for testing. The housing evaluation uses 23,287 testing households; the gold-capacity evaluation contains 23,287 eligible testing households. Other component-specific testing counts are not supplied in the wealth metrics export.
testing_notes.classification: Classification is evaluated on the shared 20% AIDIS holdout. The gold-capacity evaluation records 23,287 eligible testing households; the three-group agreement export does not provide its own eligible count.
